• Target audience & prerequisites

• Module breakdown & estimated time

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Emma Clarke, and I’m excited to welcome you to our Generative AI onboarding course.

First, let’s look at what we’ll achieve together: by the end of this course you’ll understand the basics of generative AI and large language models, know who this training is for, and see how the modules fit into the estimated time frame.
This course is designed for beginners like you, so no prior AI experience is required—just curiosity and a willingness to experiment.
We’ve broken the material into four modules, each focused on a key topic, and we’ve allocated about an hour per module to keep the pace comfortable.
To get the most out of our time, I encourage you to ask questions whenever something isn’t clear, try the hands‑on activities, and use the quick tips from our teaching assistant Liam.
Let’s get started and explore the exciting world of generative AI together!

elements.content: Module 1 – What is Generative AI?

• Definition: AI that creates new content

• Analytical AI vs Generative AI

• Real‑world examples: text, image, code generation

• Transforming workplaces: automation and creativity

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Emma Clarke, and I’m excited to start our journey into Generative AI. Today we’ll explore what Generative AI actually is and why it’s reshaping the way we work.

First, let’s look at the definition: Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that can create new content—whether it’s text, images, music, or even code—rather than just analyzing existing data.
Notice here the contrast with analytical AI, which focuses on interpreting or summarizing data. Generative AI goes a step further by actually producing fresh, original outputs.
Real‑world examples include chatbots that write articles, tools that generate artwork from prompts, and code assistants that suggest programming snippets.
These capabilities are transforming workplaces by automating creative tasks, speeding up prototyping, and unlocking new possibilities for innovation.

To recap, we’ve defined Generative AI, distinguished it from analytical AI, examined a few practical examples, and highlighted its impact on modern work environments. Let’s keep these ideas in mind as we dive deeper in the next module.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common use case for generative AI?

options.label: Creating realistic images from text descriptions
Sorting customer records alphabetically
Calculating statistical averages of data sets
Monitoring network traffic for security threats

questions.analysis: Generative AI can produce new content such as images from textual prompts. The other options describe analytical or operational tasks, not generation of new data.

questions.question: Select all statements that correctly distinguish generative AI from analytical AI:

options.label: Generative AI creates new content; analytical AI extracts insights from existing data.
Generative AI requires labeled training data; analytical AI does not.
Generative AI can be used for tasks like text summarization; analytical AI cannot.
Generative AI models often produce probabilistic outputs; analytical AI typically yields deterministic results.

questions.analysis: Statement A correctly contrasts creation versus insight extraction. Statement D is accurate because generative models generate varied outputs based on probability distributions, while many analytical models give a single best estimate. Statement B is false: both types can use labeled or unlabeled data. Statement C is false because text summarization is an analytical (extractive) task, not generative.

actions.text: Hi everyone, I'm Emma. Let’s dive into a short quiz to see how well you’ve grasped the basics of generative AI. Read each question carefully, then pick the answer that fits best.

Remember, a key use case for generative AI is creating new content—like turning a text description into a realistic image. It isn’t meant for simple sorting, calculating averages, or monitoring network traffic.

When we compare generative AI with analytical AI, keep these distinctions in mind: generative models produce fresh content and often give probabilistic results, while analytical models focus on extracting insights from existing data and usually provide deterministic outputs. Also, generative AI can handle tasks such as text summarization, whereas analytical AI is more about data analysis.

elements.content: Module 2 – Understanding Large Language Models (LLMs)

• Definition: AI model that predicts text

• Token: smallest text unit, counts toward limits

• Context: prior tokens shape the next prediction

• Next‑token prediction drives completion

actions.text: Next, let’s explore Module 2: Understanding Large Language Models, or LLMs.
First, an LLM is an AI model that predicts the next word in a sentence based on the words it has already seen.
A token is the smallest piece of text the model works with—think of it as a word fragment or punctuation mark that the model counts.
Why does the token matter? Because the model’s understanding builds token by token, so each token shapes the next prediction.
Context is everything: the surrounding tokens give the model clues about what comes next, letting it generate coherent sentences.
Finally, the core of an LLM’s work is next‑token prediction—choosing the most likely next token from all possibilities, then repeating the process.
To recap, we defined LLMs, explained tokens and their importance, saw how context guides predictions, and covered the role of next‑token prediction. Great job, everyone!

questions.question: Which of the following best defines a "token" in the context of large language models?

options.label: A piece of text, such as a word or sub‑word fragment, that the model processes as a single unit
A complete sentence that the model generates in one step
A hardware component that stores model parameters
A user’s login credential used to access the model

questions.analysis: In LLMs, a token is the smallest textual unit the model works with, often a word, sub‑word, or character. The other options describe unrelated concepts.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of providing context (prompt) to a large language model?

options.label: To set a limit on the number of tokens the model can generate
To give the model information that guides its predictions toward relevant and coherent output
To train the model on new data during inference
To encrypt the model’s internal weights for security

questions.analysis: Context supplies the model with the necessary background or instructions, enabling it to produce responses that are on‑topic and logically consistent. The other options describe unrelated functionalities.

actions.text: Alright, let’s see how well you’ve grasped the basics we just covered about tokens and context in large language models.
Remember, a token is simply a piece of text—a word or even part of a word—that the model reads and processes as one unit. It’s not a whole sentence or any hardware component.

And the context, or prompt, is what you give the model before it generates a response. That context guides the model’s predictions, helping it produce output that’s relevant and coherent to your request.
Take your time, read each question carefully, and choose the answer that best matches these definitions.

elements.content: Module 3 – How LLMs Are Built

• Sources of training data

• Pre‑training vs. fine‑tuning

• Instruction tuning and benefits

• Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)

• Cost and infrastructure considerations

actions.text: All right, everyone, let's dive into Module 3: How large language models are built.
First, we need to consider where the training data comes from—everything from books and web pages to code repositories and user interactions.
Next, there’s a key distinction: pre‑training gives the model a broad understanding of language, while fine‑tuning adjusts it for a specific task or domain.
Instruction tuning goes a step further by teaching the model to follow human instructions more reliably, which improves usefulness and safety.
Finally, reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, lets us fine‑tune the model using real‑world feedback loops, helping it generate better, more accurate responses.
Keep in mind that all these steps require substantial compute power and infrastructure, which influences the cost and accessibility of building LLMs.
To recap, we covered data sources, the difference between pre‑training and fine‑tuning, instruction tuning, RLHF, and the practical considerations of cost and hardware.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of fine‑tuning a large language model?

options.label: To adapt the model to a specific task or domain using additional labeled data
To reduce the total number of parameters in the model
To increase the model's token limit for longer inputs
To replace the need for any pre‑training phase

questions.analysis: Fine‑tuning adds task‑specific supervision so the pretrained model can perform well on a particular application. The other options describe unrelated effects.

questions.question: Which sentence best describes Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)?

options.label: The model is trained to maximize a reward signal that reflects human preferences on its outputs
The model learns to generate data by predicting the next word in a large corpus
The model is compressed to run faster on edge devices using human annotations
The model automatically writes code without any human input

questions.analysis: RLHF uses human feedback to create a reward model, guiding the language model to produce outputs that align with human judgments. The other statements describe unrelated training methods.

actions.text: Hi everyone! It’s Emma. Let’s put what we just covered about building large language models to the test with a quick two‑question quiz.

Remember, fine‑tuning is all about taking a pre‑trained model and teaching it to perform well on a specific task or domain by feeding it extra labeled examples. It doesn’t shrink the model or change its token limit—it simply adapts its knowledge.

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, or RLHF, means we let the model generate answers, then humans rank those answers. The model then learns to maximize a reward signal that reflects those human preferences. In one sentence: RLHF trains the model to produce outputs that people judge as more useful or appropriate.
Take a moment to read each question carefully, pick the best answer, and trust your intuition—if you’re unsure, think back to the explanations we just reviewed.

actions.topic: How does fine‑tuning differ from RLHF, and why might you choose one approach over the other?
actions.prompt: Consider practical scenarios where each method shines. Share any uncertainties you still have.

elements.content: Module 4 – Transformers Simplified

• Origin of transformers

• Core idea of self‑attention

• How attention creates contextual representations

• Why transformers replaced older models

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Emma Clarke, and today we’re going to demystify transformers—one of the most powerful ideas in modern AI.
First, let’s look at the origins of transformers. Back in 2017, researchers wanted a model that could handle whole sentences at once, instead of processing words step by step like older RNNs.
The core idea that made this possible is self‑attention—letting each word look at every other word to decide which parts are most important for its meaning.
By applying self‑attention repeatedly, the model builds contextual representations, meaning each word’s meaning is shaped by the whole sentence around it.
Because transformers can capture context so efficiently, they quickly replaced older models in tasks like translation, summarization, and even image processing.

So, to recap: we’ve covered where transformers came from, how self‑attention works, how it creates rich context, and why it became the go‑to architecture for many AI problems. Let’s keep this foundation in mind as we dive deeper in the next modules.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the self‑attention mechanism in a transformer?

options.label: Each word gathers information from all other words in the same sentence to compute a new representation for itself.
Each word is compared only with the first word of the sentence to decide its importance.
Each word is processed independently without looking at any other words.
Each word is replaced by a fixed lookup table entry regardless of context.

questions.analysis: Self‑attention allows every token to attend to (i.e., weigh and combine) information from all other tokens in the same sequence, producing a context‑aware representation. Options B, C, and D describe mechanisms that do not involve mutual interaction among tokens, so they are incorrect.

questions.question: What is a commonly cited limitation of current transformer models?

options.label: They require very large amounts of labeled data for every new task.
Their computational cost grows quadratically with sequence length, making long inputs expensive.
They cannot be trained on GPU hardware due to memory constraints.
They are unable to handle any kind of sequential data.

questions.analysis: The attention matrix in a transformer has size proportional to the square of the sequence length, leading to quadratic time and memory requirements. This makes processing long sequences costly. Option A is partially true for some tasks but not the primary architectural limitation. Options C and D are false; transformers are routinely trained on GPUs and excel with sequential data.

actions.text: Hi everyone! Let’s see how well you’ve grasped the basics of self‑attention and the main limitation of today’s transformer models.

Recall that self‑attention lets each word look at every other word in the same sentence and blend that information into a new representation—think of it as a group chat where every participant contributes to each other’s understanding. A common stumbling block is to think the words act alone; that’s not how attention works.

Also, remember that transformers become pricey as sentences get longer because the amount of calculation grows with the square of the sequence length. This makes processing very long texts computationally expensive.

Take a moment to read each question carefully, pick the answer that best matches the concepts we just reviewed, and don’t worry if you need to think it through—these quiz items are designed to reinforce your learning.

actions.topic: Why does the quadratic cost of self‑attention matter for real‑world applications?
actions.prompt: Consider examples like long documents or video transcripts, and discuss possible strategies to address this limitation.

elements.content: Module 5 – Real‑World Use Cases

• Assisted writing & summarization

• Translation & multilingual support

• Text classification & semantic search

• Chatbots for business operations

• Code generation & developer assistance

• Educational support & tutoring

actions.text: Now we’ll explore real‑world use cases for large language models. This module highlights how these tools can help us in daily tasks and across industries.
First, assisted writing and summarization. LLMs can draft emails, create reports, or condense long articles into clear summaries, saving us time and effort.
Second, translation and multilingual support. These models can translate text between many languages instantly, helping businesses communicate globally.
Third, text classification and semantic search. By understanding the meaning behind words, LLMs can organize documents and retrieve relevant information more accurately.
Fourth, chatbots for business operations. Automated agents can handle customer inquiries, schedule appointments, and provide support 24/7.
Fifth, code generation and developer assistance. LLMs can suggest code snippets, debug errors, and speed up software development.
Finally, educational support and tutoring. These models act as personal tutors, offering explanations, practice problems, and instant feedback for learners.

To recap, we’ve seen how LLMs assist with writing, translate languages, classify and search content, power business chatbots, help developers code, and support education. These examples illustrate the versatility of large language models in real‑world settings.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate use case for an LLM's code generation capability?

options.label: Automatically writing unit tests for a newly created function
Translating a marketing brochure into another language
Summarizing a long research article into a short abstract
Generating a visual design mock‑up for a mobile app

questions.analysis: LLMs excel at generating syntactically correct code snippets and can quickly produce unit tests based on code context. The other options involve translation, summarization, or visual design, which are not primary strengths of code‑generation models.

questions.question: Select all scenarios where summarization by an LLM adds clear business value (choose all that apply).

options.label: Providing a brief overview of daily sales reports for senior managers
Creating detailed line‑by‑line code comments for a legacy codebase
Transforming a lengthy customer support transcript into key issue bullet points
Generating a full legal contract from scratch

questions.analysis: Summarization helps condense large textual data into concise insights, which is valuable for sales report overviews (A) and extracting key points from support transcripts (C). Writing detailed code comments (B) and drafting full contracts (D) require creation rather than condensation, so summarization is not the primary benefit.

actions.text: Hi everyone! It’s Emma here. Let’s dive into a quick quiz to see how well you can match large‑language‑model capabilities with real‑world business tasks.

Read each question carefully and pick the answer that best reflects the strength of the LLM. Remember, think about what the model does best—generating code, translating language, summarising text, or creating visual designs.

For the first question, focus on where code generation truly shines. LLMs excel at writing snippets of code that fit a clear specification, like creating unit tests for a fresh function. They’re not yet reliable for full visual mock‑ups or nuanced legal drafting.

In the second question, consider where a concise summary saves time for busy stakeholders. Turning long sales reports into a brief overview, or distilling a customer‑support transcript into key issues, both deliver clear business value. Detailed code comments or drafting an entire contract are better suited to other tools.

actions.topic: How can we decide which LLM capability to apply in a new project?
actions.prompt: Think about the specific problem you’re trying to solve and match it to the strengths we discussed.

elements.content: Module 6 – Prompt Engineering Basics

• What a prompt is and why it matters

• Vague vs. precise prompts

• Role, goal, context, format, constraints

• Iterative testing and refinement

actions.text: Welcome, everyone! I'm Emma, and today we'll dive into Module 6 – Prompt Engineering Basics. We'll explore what a prompt is, why it matters, and how to craft clear, effective prompts for better AI responses.
First, let's look at the main topics on this slide. A prompt is the instruction you give to a language model, and a well‑written prompt guides the model toward the answer you need.
Notice the bullet that mentions vague versus precise prompts. Vague prompts leave the model guessing, while precise prompts define the role, goal, context, format, and any constraints.

Think of adding a role like "You are a friendly travel guide," a clear goal such as "Provide a 3‑day itinerary for Paris," relevant context, the desired format, and any constraints like "under 500 words." This structure helps the model deliver exactly what you need.
Finally, remember that prompt engineering is an iterative process. Test your prompt, review the output, refine wording, and repeat until the results match your expectations.

actions.prompt: Share an example of a vague prompt you used and how you might improve it.

elements.content: Module 7 – Limits, Risks, and Governance

• Hallucination: plausible but incorrect output

• Biases inherited from training data

• Confidentiality and data‑protection concerns

• Intellectual‑property considerations

• Human validation as a safety net

• Corporate‑governance guidelines

actions.text: Alright, let’s dive into Module 7: Limits, Risks, and Governance. This part of our journey explores the important safety and ethical considerations when working with AI.
First, hallucination – that’s when an AI generates information that sounds plausible but is actually incorrect. Think of it as an imaginative storyteller that sometimes invents facts.
Second, biases inherited from the training data. If the data contains stereotypes or imbalances, the model can unintentionally repeat them.
Third, confidentiality and data‑protection concerns. We must be careful not to feed sensitive personal or corporate information into the model.
Fourth, intellectual‑property considerations – AI can unintentionally reproduce copyrighted material, so we need clear usage policies.
Fifth, human validation as a safety net. Even with strong models, a person should always review critical outputs before they’re used.
Finally, corporate governance guidelines help embed these safeguards into policies, training, and accountability structures.
To recap, we covered hallucinations, bias, privacy, IP, human checks, and governance. Keep these points in mind as you design and deploy AI solutions responsibly.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the primary risk associated with large language model (LLM) hallucination?

options.label: The model generates plausible‑looking content that is factually incorrect or unsupported
The model refuses to produce any output for sensitive topics
The model requires excessive computational resources for inference
The model always repeats the exact same response to similar prompts

questions.analysis: Hallucination means the LLM creates statements that sound credible but are false or have no basis in its training data. The other options describe different issues (refusal, compute cost, repetition) but not hallucination.

questions.question: Which governance practice is recommended to mitigate the risk of LLM hallucination in a production environment?

options.label: Deploy the model without human review to speed up delivery
Implement a post‑generation fact‑checking layer before releasing outputs
Use only the largest available model regardless of cost
Restrict model usage to internal developers only, without policies

questions.analysis: A fact‑checking or verification step after generation helps catch hallucinated statements before they reach users. The other choices either remove safeguards or add unnecessary constraints without addressing hallucination.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let's see how well you grasped today's topic on LLM risks and governance. We'll go through two quick questions that focus on the core risk of hallucination and a practical way to govern it in production.

Remember, the biggest danger with hallucination is that the model can sound convincing while actually delivering false or unverified information. Keep that in mind as you choose the best answer for the first question.
For the second question, think about how we can catch those mistakes before they reach users. A post‑generation fact‑checking step is a simple but effective safeguard.

actions.topic: How can we balance the speed of deploying LLMs with the need for reliable, accurate outputs?
actions.prompt: Share a situation where you might need a fact‑checking layer and any challenges you foresee.

elements.content: Module 8 – Hands‑On Activity

• Compare a weak prompt vs. a strong prompt

• Rewrite a prompt for clearer intent

• Generate two model outputs and evaluate accuracy, clarity, risk

• Document findings and improvement ideas

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let’s dive into our hands‑on activity for Module 8.
First, we’ll compare a weak prompt with a strong one, seeing how clarity and detail affect the model’s response.
Next, you’ll rewrite a given prompt to make its intent crystal‑clear, applying the tips we’ve discussed.
Then, generate two model outputs—one from the original prompt and one from your revised version— and evaluate them on accuracy, clarity, and any potential risk.
Finally, document what you discovered and note any ideas for further improvement. Feel free to ask questions as you work through each step!

questions.question: Based on the revised prompt you created, list at least two specific improvements you made to the original prompt and explain how each change enhances clarity or usability.

questions.question: Evaluate the three sample responses generated from the revised prompt and select the most reliable one. Justify your choice using the evaluation criteria of format compliance, answer accuracy, and explanation completeness.

actions.text: Alright, let's move on to our practical exercise review. This short quiz will ask you to reflect on the prompt you just refined and to evaluate the sample responses we generated.

Remember, you need to identify at least two concrete improvements you made to the original prompt—think about wording, structure, or added constraints—and explain how each change makes the prompt clearer or more usable.

For the second question, compare the three sample answers. Choose the one that best follows the evaluation criteria—correct format, accurate content, and a complete explanation—then justify your choice.

blocks.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Emma Clarke, and I’m excited to start our journey into Generative AI. Today we’ll explore what Generative AI actually is and why it’s reshaping the way we work.

First, let’s look at the definition: Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that can create new content—whether it’s text, images, music, or even code—rather than just analyzing existing data.
Notice here the contrast with analytical AI, which focuses on interpreting or summarizing data. Generative AI goes a step further by actually producing fresh, original outputs.
Real‑world examples include chatbots that write articles, tools that generate artwork from prompts, and code assistants that suggest programming snippets.
These capabilities are transforming workplaces by automating creative tasks, speeding up prototyping, and unlocking new possibilities for innovation.

To recap, we’ve defined Generative AI, distinguished it from analytical AI, examined a few practical examples, and highlighted its impact on modern work environments. Let’s keep these ideas in mind as we dive deeper in the next module.

blocks.question: Which of the following is a common use case for generative AI?
blocks.explanation: Generative AI can produce new content such as images from textual prompts. The other options describe analytical or operational tasks, not generation of new data.

options.label: Creating realistic images from text descriptions
Sorting customer records alphabetically
Calculating statistical averages of data sets
Monitoring network traffic for security threats

blocks.question: Select all statements that correctly distinguish generative AI from analytical AI:
blocks.explanation: Statement A correctly contrasts creation versus insight extraction. Statement D is accurate because generative models generate varied outputs based on probability distributions, while many analytical models give a single best estimate. Statement B is false: both types can use labeled or unlabeled data. Statement C is false because text summarization is an analytical (extractive) task, not generative.

options.label: Generative AI creates new content; analytical AI extracts insights from existing data.
Generative AI requires labeled training data; analytical AI does not.
Generative AI can be used for tasks like text summarization; analytical AI cannot.
Generative AI models often produce probabilistic outputs; analytical AI typically yields deterministic results.

blocks.text: Hi everyone, I'm Emma. Let’s dive into a short quiz to see how well you’ve grasped the basics of generative AI. Read each question carefully, then pick the answer that fits best.

Remember, a key use case for generative AI is creating new content—like turning a text description into a realistic image. It isn’t meant for simple sorting, calculating averages, or monitoring network traffic.

When we compare generative AI with analytical AI, keep these distinctions in mind: generative models produce fresh content and often give probabilistic results, while analytical models focus on extracting insights from existing data and usually provide deterministic outputs. Also, generative AI can handle tasks such as text summarization, whereas analytical AI is more about data analysis.

blocks.text: Next, let’s explore Module 2: Understanding Large Language Models, or LLMs.
First, an LLM is an AI model that predicts the next word in a sentence based on the words it has already seen.
A token is the smallest piece of text the model works with—think of it as a word fragment or punctuation mark that the model counts.
Why does the token matter? Because the model’s understanding builds token by token, so each token shapes the next prediction.
Context is everything: the surrounding tokens give the model clues about what comes next, letting it generate coherent sentences.
Finally, the core of an LLM’s work is next‑token prediction—choosing the most likely next token from all possibilities, then repeating the process.
To recap, we defined LLMs, explained tokens and their importance, saw how context guides predictions, and covered the role of next‑token prediction. Great job, everyone!

blocks.question: Which of the following best defines a "token" in the context of large language models?
blocks.explanation: In LLMs, a token is the smallest textual unit the model works with, often a word, sub‑word, or character. The other options describe unrelated concepts.

options.label: A piece of text, such as a word or sub‑word fragment, that the model processes as a single unit
A complete sentence that the model generates in one step
A hardware component that stores model parameters
A user’s login credential used to access the model

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of providing context (prompt) to a large language model?
blocks.explanation: Context supplies the model with the necessary background or instructions, enabling it to produce responses that are on‑topic and logically consistent. The other options describe unrelated functionalities.

options.label: To set a limit on the number of tokens the model can generate
To give the model information that guides its predictions toward relevant and coherent output
To train the model on new data during inference
To encrypt the model’s internal weights for security

blocks.text: Alright, let’s see how well you’ve grasped the basics we just covered about tokens and context in large language models.
Remember, a token is simply a piece of text—a word or even part of a word—that the model reads and processes as one unit. It’s not a whole sentence or any hardware component.

And the context, or prompt, is what you give the model before it generates a response. That context guides the model’s predictions, helping it produce output that’s relevant and coherent to your request.
Take your time, read each question carefully, and choose the answer that best matches these definitions.

blocks.text: All right, everyone, let's dive into Module 3: How large language models are built.
First, we need to consider where the training data comes from—everything from books and web pages to code repositories and user interactions.
Next, there’s a key distinction: pre‑training gives the model a broad understanding of language, while fine‑tuning adjusts it for a specific task or domain.
Instruction tuning goes a step further by teaching the model to follow human instructions more reliably, which improves usefulness and safety.
Finally, reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, lets us fine‑tune the model using real‑world feedback loops, helping it generate better, more accurate responses.
Keep in mind that all these steps require substantial compute power and infrastructure, which influences the cost and accessibility of building LLMs.
To recap, we covered data sources, the difference between pre‑training and fine‑tuning, instruction tuning, RLHF, and the practical considerations of cost and hardware.

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of fine‑tuning a large language model?
blocks.explanation: Fine‑tuning adds task‑specific supervision so the pretrained model can perform well on a particular application. The other options describe unrelated effects.

options.label: To adapt the model to a specific task or domain using additional labeled data

options.label: The model is trained to maximize a reward signal that reflects human preferences on its outputs
The model learns to generate data by predicting the next word in a large corpus
The model is compressed to run faster on edge devices using human annotations
The model automatically writes code without any human input

blocks.text: Hi everyone! It’s Emma. Let’s put what we just covered about building large language models to the test with a quick two‑question quiz.

Remember, fine‑tuning is all about taking a pre‑trained model and teaching it to perform well on a specific task or domain by feeding it extra labeled examples. It doesn’t shrink the model or change its token limit—it simply adapts its knowledge.

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, or RLHF, means we let the model generate answers, then humans rank those answers. The model then learns to maximize a reward signal that reflects those human preferences. In one sentence: RLHF trains the model to produce outputs that people judge as more useful or appropriate.
Take a moment to read each question carefully, pick the best answer, and trust your intuition—if you’re unsure, think back to the explanations we just reviewed.

blocks.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Emma Clarke, and today we’re going to demystify transformers—one of the most powerful ideas in modern AI.
First, let’s look at the origins of transformers. Back in 2017, researchers wanted a model that could handle whole sentences at once, instead of processing words step by step like older RNNs.
The core idea that made this possible is self‑attention—letting each word look at every other word to decide which parts are most important for its meaning.
By applying self‑attention repeatedly, the model builds contextual representations, meaning each word’s meaning is shaped by the whole sentence around it.
Because transformers can capture context so efficiently, they quickly replaced older models in tasks like translation, summarization, and even image processing.

So, to recap: we’ve covered where transformers came from, how self‑attention works, how it creates rich context, and why it became the go‑to architecture for many AI problems. Let’s keep this foundation in mind as we dive deeper in the next modules.

blocks.question: Which of the following best describes the self‑attention mechanism in a transformer?
blocks.explanation: Self‑attention allows every token to attend to (i.e., weigh and combine) information from all other tokens in the same sequence, producing a context‑aware representation. Options B, C, and D describe mechanisms that do not involve mutual interaction among tokens, so they are incorrect.

options.label: Each word gathers information from all other words in the same sentence to compute a new representation for itself.
Each word is compared only with the first word of the sentence to decide its importance.
Each word is processed independently without looking at any other words.
Each word is replaced by a fixed lookup table entry regardless of context.

blocks.question: What is a commonly cited limitation of current transformer models?
blocks.explanation: The attention matrix in a transformer has size proportional to the square of the sequence length, leading to quadratic time and memory requirements. This makes processing long sequences costly. Option A is partially true for some tasks but not the primary architectural limitation. Options C and D are false; transformers are routinely trained on GPUs and excel with sequential data.

options.label: They require very large amounts of labeled data for every new task.
Their computational cost grows quadratically with sequence length, making long inputs expensive.
They cannot be trained on GPU hardware due to memory constraints.
They are unable to handle any kind of sequential data.

blocks.text: Hi everyone! Let’s see how well you’ve grasped the basics of self‑attention and the main limitation of today’s transformer models.

Recall that self‑attention lets each word look at every other word in the same sentence and blend that information into a new representation—think of it as a group chat where every participant contributes to each other’s understanding. A common stumbling block is to think the words act alone; that’s not how attention works.

Also, remember that transformers become pricey as sentences get longer because the amount of calculation grows with the square of the sequence length. This makes processing very long texts computationally expensive.

Take a moment to read each question carefully, pick the answer that best matches the concepts we just reviewed, and don’t worry if you need to think it through—these quiz items are designed to reinforce your learning.

blocks.text: Now we’ll explore real‑world use cases for large language models. This module highlights how these tools can help us in daily tasks and across industries.
First, assisted writing and summarization. LLMs can draft emails, create reports, or condense long articles into clear summaries, saving us time and effort.
Second, translation and multilingual support. These models can translate text between many languages instantly, helping businesses communicate globally.
Third, text classification and semantic search. By understanding the meaning behind words, LLMs can organize documents and retrieve relevant information more accurately.
Fourth, chatbots for business operations. Automated agents can handle customer inquiries, schedule appointments, and provide support 24/7.
Fifth, code generation and developer assistance. LLMs can suggest code snippets, debug errors, and speed up software development.
Finally, educational support and tutoring. These models act as personal tutors, offering explanations, practice problems, and instant feedback for learners.

To recap, we’ve seen how LLMs assist with writing, translate languages, classify and search content, power business chatbots, help developers code, and support education. These examples illustrate the versatility of large language models in real‑world settings.

For the first question, focus on where code generation truly shines. LLMs excel at writing snippets of code that fit a clear specification, like creating unit tests for a fresh function. They’re not yet reliable for full visual mock‑ups or nuanced legal drafting.

In the second question, consider where a concise summary saves time for busy stakeholders. Turning long sales reports into a brief overview, or distilling a customer‑support transcript into key issues, both deliver clear business value. Detailed code comments or drafting an entire contract are better suited to other tools.

blocks.text: Welcome, everyone! I'm Emma, and today we'll dive into Module 6 – Prompt Engineering Basics. We'll explore what a prompt is, why it matters, and how to craft clear, effective prompts for better AI responses.
First, let's look at the main topics on this slide. A prompt is the instruction you give to a language model, and a well‑written prompt guides the model toward the answer you need.
Notice the bullet that mentions vague versus precise prompts. Vague prompts leave the model guessing, while precise prompts define the role, goal, context, format, and any constraints.

Think of adding a role like "You are a friendly travel guide," a clear goal such as "Provide a 3‑day itinerary for Paris," relevant context, the desired format, and any constraints like "under 500 words." This structure helps the model deliver exactly what you need.
Finally, remember that prompt engineering is an iterative process. Test your prompt, review the output, refine wording, and repeat until the results match your expectations.

blocks.text: Alright, let’s dive into Module 7: Limits, Risks, and Governance. This part of our journey explores the important safety and ethical considerations when working with AI.
First, hallucination – that’s when an AI generates information that sounds plausible but is actually incorrect. Think of it as an imaginative storyteller that sometimes invents facts.
Second, biases inherited from the training data. If the data contains stereotypes or imbalances, the model can unintentionally repeat them.
Third, confidentiality and data‑protection concerns. We must be careful not to feed sensitive personal or corporate information into the model.
Fourth, intellectual‑property considerations – AI can unintentionally reproduce copyrighted material, so we need clear usage policies.
Fifth, human validation as a safety net. Even with strong models, a person should always review critical outputs before they’re used.
Finally, corporate governance guidelines help embed these safeguards into policies, training, and accountability structures.
To recap, we covered hallucinations, bias, privacy, IP, human checks, and governance. Keep these points in mind as you design and deploy AI solutions responsibly.

blocks.question: Which of the following describes the primary risk associated with large language model (LLM) hallucination?
blocks.explanation: Hallucination means the LLM creates statements that sound credible but are false or have no basis in its training data. The other options describe different issues (refusal, compute cost, repetition) but not hallucination.

options.label: The model generates plausible‑looking content that is factually incorrect or unsupported

blocks.question: Which governance practice is recommended to mitigate the risk of LLM hallucination in a production environment?
blocks.explanation: A fact‑checking or verification step after generation helps catch hallucinated statements before they reach users. The other choices either remove safeguards or add unnecessary constraints without addressing hallucination.

options.label: Deploy the model without human review to speed up delivery
Implement a post‑generation fact‑checking layer before releasing outputs
Use only the largest available model regardless of cost
Restrict model usage to internal developers only, without policies

blocks.text: Alright, everyone, let's see how well you grasped today's topic on LLM risks and governance. We'll go through two quick questions that focus on the core risk of hallucination and a practical way to govern it in production.

Remember, the biggest danger with hallucination is that the model can sound convincing while actually delivering false or unverified information. Keep that in mind as you choose the best answer for the first question.
For the second question, think about how we can catch those mistakes before they reach users. A post‑generation fact‑checking step is a simple but effective safeguard.

blocks.explanation: In the first week, the employee must ensure access to tools (A) and finish required safety training (D). The product deep‑dive (B) is scheduled for week two, and performance reports (C) are not due until later.

options.label: Set up their workstation and log into core systems
Attend the product deep‑dive training session
Submit their first quarterly performance report
Complete the mandatory workplace safety module

blocks.question: What is the primary benefit of using the company's internal knowledge base?
blocks.explanation: The knowledge base is meant to provide a single source of current information, helping employees find answers quickly. It does not affect promotion speed, replace live training, or monitor communications.

options.label: It guarantees faster promotions
It centralizes up‑to‑date information for quick reference
It replaces the need for any live training sessions
It automatically records all employee communications

blocks.question: Which metrics are used in the onboarding effectiveness dashboard? (select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: The dashboard tracks operational metrics: how quickly new hires access systems (A), completion of required compliance training (B), and whether they stay beyond the initial period (D). Salary expectations are not a dashboard metric.

options.label: Average time to first login
Number of completed compliance modules
Employee's personal salary expectations
Retention rate after 90 days

blocks.question: Explain how a mentor can support a new employee during the onboarding period.
blocks.explanation: A strong answer mentions that a mentor helps the newcomer understand day‑to‑day responsibilities, introduces them to team norms and company values, and schedules regular feedback sessions to track progress and address questions.

blocks.text: Great job getting through the onboarding modules! Now it's time for a quick validation quiz to see how well you've absorbed the key concepts.

Remember, the welcome module is all about introducing you to our company culture and essential policies—not technical specs or sales targets. Keep that in mind as you select the best answer for each question.

When you think about the first week, focus on the practical steps: setting up your workstation, logging into core systems, attending the product deep‑dive, and completing the mandatory safety module. Anything beyond that, like performance reports, comes later.

The internal knowledge base is your go‑to resource for up‑to‑date information, helping you find answers quickly without replacing live training. And the onboarding effectiveness dashboard tracks things like average time to first login, completed compliance modules, and 90‑day retention rates.
